attempts.instructions:
This server reproduces Open WebUI's internet-search architecture: ONE stable tool contract
(search_web, fetch_url) with multiple provider adapters routed behind it — not a separate tool
surface per provider. You do not choose a provider in the normal case; the server picks one
automatically with real fallback, and tells you which one it used.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
PROVIDER ROUTING — handled by this server, not by you
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
search_web automatically routes requests across currently enabled internet-search providers.
Do not select or assume a provider, and do not assume a fixed provider order — which providers
are enabled and in what priority can change (a provider can be added, removed, or disabled
without this text being updated). Inspect the response's `provider_used` and `attempts` fields
after every call to see exactly what happened: which providers were tried, in what order, why
any were skipped or failed, and which one actually answered. Call get_provider_status() if you
need to know ahead of time which providers are currently enabled. You CAN force a specific
provider via the `provider` parameter if you have a reason to (e.g. re-querying after a
free-tier answer wasn't good enough).

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
SEARCH DEPTH — mode parameter
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
- mode="discover" — broad exploratory search. Returns titles/URLs/snippets only, no page
  content fetched. Use when scanning a topic before narrowing down.
- mode="answer" — for answering, explaining, comparing, or summarizing. Fetches full page
  content inline for the top results (fetch_top_n, default 10).
- mode="auto" (default) — the server infers depth from the query using a small, deterministic
  heuristic (question marks, comparison/explanation cue words, or query length lean toward
  "answer"; short/broad queries lean toward "discover"). This is a heuristic, not true intent
  understanding — pass mode explicitly when you know which you want.
- fetch_top_n is still available as an advanced override and always wins over mode when set
  explicitly.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
REQUIRED USAGE PATTERN: agentic search, NOT single-shot tool calling
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
1. QUERY DELIBERATELY — focused queries for multi-part questions, run several rather than one
   broad query.
2. EVALUATE, don't trust blindly — read titles/snippets/domains critically. Whichever provider
   was used, snippets are a pointer to a source, not verified evidence.
3. READ extracted_text FIRST when content_status is "fetched" or "partially_fetched" — do NOT
   make a redundant fetch_url call for a URL search_web already fetched. Only use fetch_url
   for: a URL beyond the fetched range, a different max_chars, re-fetching a URL from an
   earlier turn, content_status was "not_requested"/"fetch_failed", or a specific direct URL
   needs inspecting.
4. ITERATE if results are poor — reformulate the query, or try fetch_url on a known/guessed
   direct URL (e.g. a manufacturer's own spec page) instead of searching at all, especially
   for time-sensitive or fact-specific questions. Prefer direct, authoritative source pages
   over search snippets for time-sensitive facts.
5. Cite your sources in the final answer (title/URL).
6. Do NOT treat an empty result as proof information doesn't exist — check `attempts` and each
   attempt's failure_code/reason first; an empty result can mean every provider errored, not
   that nothing was found.

Tools:
- search_web(query, mode="auto", provider=None, max_results=5, fetch_top_n=None, min_results=None,
  max_chars=None) -> {results: [{link, title, snippet, extracted_text, content_status,
  fetch_method, fetch_error, retrieved_at}], provider_used, attempts} — content_status is one
  of not_requested/fetched/partially_fetched/fetch_failed/blocked/unsupported. min_results, if
  set, escalates to the next provider when a result set is thinner than requested.
- fetch_url(urls, max_chars=None) -> [{source_id, title, final_url, extracted_text,
  retrieved_at, status, error?}] — SSRF-protected: URLs resolving to localhost/private IPs/
  cloud-metadata addresses are refused and reported with status "blocked", not fetched. Same
  SSRF protection applies to any URL search_web auto-fetches.
- get_provider_status() -> [{provider, enabled, cost_class, routing_priority, healthy}] —
  diagnostic only, does not select a provider or perform a search.

tools.name: search_web
tools.title: Search Web
tools.description:
Search the web. Routes to a provider adapter automatically (currently enabled providers,
real fallback) unless `provider` is explicitly set. mode controls search depth:
"discover" (snippets only), "answer" (fetches full page content inline for the top
fetch_top_n results, default 10), or "auto" (default -- a deterministic heuristic infers
depth from the query; see AGENT_INSTRUCTIONS). fetch_top_n, if set explicitly, always
overrides mode. min_results, if set, escalates to the next provider when a result set is
thinner than requested. Returns {results: [{link, title, snippet, extracted_text,
content_status, fetch_method, fetch_error, retrieved_at}], provider_used, attempts} --
content_status is one of not_requested/fetched/partially_fetched/fetch_failed/blocked/
unsupported. Check provider_used/attempts to see what actually happened, don't assume.
Content is fetched in provider-returned order, not ranked/reranked -- that judgment stays
with you.

tools.name: fetch_url
tools.title: Fetch Url
tools.description:
Fetch and extract full page content for one or more URLs (e.g. from search_web's
results, or a URL you already know). SSRF-protected: any URL resolving to localhost, a
private IP range, or a cloud-metadata address is refused, not fetched, and reported with
status "blocked" and a reason. Returns one entry per URL, same order given.

tools.name: get_provider_status
tools.title: Get Provider Status
tools.description:
Diagnostic status for every internet-search provider this server knows about: whether
it's currently enabled/in the routing chain, its cost class (free/paid), routing priority,
and (if probe=True) a real lightweight live health check. Does NOT select a provider or
perform a search -- purely informational, e.g. to confirm searxng is disabled before
wondering why it never appears in attempts.

attempts.instructions:
This server drives one real Chromium browser session via Playwright and exposes it as 7
low-level browser actions: open_browser, visit_website, login, click_button, fill_form,
extract_data, close_browser. There is no higher-level "do task X on this site" tool -- you plan
the sequence of actions yourself.

REQUIRED SESSION LIFECYCLE:
1. open_browser() first -- every other tool operates on the one browser session this creates;
   calling anything else before it, or calling open_browser() again while one is already open,
   fails with a clear error rather than silently doing something unexpected.
2. visit_website(url), then whatever sequence of click_button/fill_form/login/extract_data the
   task needs.
3. close_browser() when done -- this is not automatic; an unclosed session stays open
   consuming a real browser process until you close it or the server restarts.
Single global session: there is exactly one browser/page for the whole server, not one per
caller or per task -- do not assume you can run two unrelated browsing tasks concurrently
against this server.

FINDING SELECTORS -- this server takes real CSS selectors, not accessibility-tree refs or
natural-language element descriptions:
- You are not given the page's HTML or a structured accessibility snapshot up front. Call
  extract_data() with no selector first to read the page's visible text and orient yourself,
  then extract_data(selector) to confirm a specific CSS selector actually matches before using
  it in click_button/fill_form/login -- do not guess a selector and act on it blind.
- click_button/fill_form/login all fail with a clear error if the selector matches nothing;
  read the error rather than retrying the same selector.

TOOL SELECTION:
- Use login() (not fill_form + click_button separately) when you have a username, password,
  and their form selectors -- it is the same underlying action but tracked as one step.
- Use fill_form() for multi-field forms in one call (search boxes, checkout forms, etc.);
  fields maps CSS selector -> value, with an optional submit_selector to click afterward.
- Use click_button() for any single click that isn't a form submit already covered by
  fill_form/login (links, dropdown toggles, "load more" buttons, etc.).
- Native <select> dropdowns (e.g. e-commerce variant/option pickers) are not reliably driven by
  click_button -- if a selector looks like a <select> and click_button doesn't produce the
  expected page change, that's a real, known gap in this tool surface, not a sign you used the
  wrong selector.

SECURITY, HONEST SCOPING:
- login() takes credentials directly as call arguments. They are not stored server-side and
  are never logged by this server, but they do flow through whatever MCP client/LLM is
  orchestrating this call -- do not use this with production or high-value credentials.
- This server does not sandbox or restrict which sites visit_website can reach -- there is no
  SSRF/domain allowlist here unlike this project family's search/document servers. Treat it as
  operating with the same access as whoever is running it, not as safe-by-default for
  untrusted or adversarial target sites.
- No screenshots, no file downloads, no PDF export -- extract_data returns text only (full
  visible body text, or matching elements' text + count for a given selector).

tools.name: open_browser
tools.title: Open Browser
tools.description: Launch a new browser session (Chromium). Must be called before any other tool.

tools.name: visit_website
tools.title: Visit Website
tools.description: Navigate the current browser session to a URL.

tools.name: login
tools.title: Login
tools.description:
Fill and submit a login form. Provide CSS selectors for the username
field, password field, and submit button (inspect the page with
extract_data first if these aren't already known).

Security: credentials are passed directly as arguments, not stored
server-side. Do not use with production/high-value credentials.

tools.name: click_button
tools.title: Click Button
tools.description: Click an element matching a CSS selector.

tools.name: fill_form
tools.title: Fill Form
tools.description:
Fill multiple form fields in one call. `fields` maps CSS selector to the
value to enter. If submit_selector is provided, clicks it afterward.

tools.name: extract_data
tools.title: Extract Data
tools.description:
Extract data from the current page. Without a selector, returns the
full visible body text. With a CSS selector, returns matching elements'
text content and count.

attempts.instructions:
This server provides scholarly research capability: search across open scholarly APIs
(OpenAlex, Crossref, arXiv, PubMed, Semantic Scholar), reconcile/deduplicate/rank results,
resolve where full content is legitimately available, and -- only when actually needed --
acquire and process that content. It exposes 7 research-level tools, not one tool per provider
or per acquisition method; provider and acquisition-tier selection are internal decisions you
never need to make directly.

CORE PRINCIPLES:
1. API-first, metadata-before-content. search_research/get_research_work never fetch full
   text -- only resolve_research_access (checks where) and retrieve_research_content (actually
   fetches) touch real content, and resolve comes before retrieve, always.
2. Don't acquire every result. Retrieve full content only for the specific works you actually
   need to answer the request, not everything a search returned.
3. Never treat a metadata record or abstract as full-text evidence, and never imply you read a
   paper when you only saw its metadata or abstract.
4. Never fabricate missing abstracts, methods, findings, or conclusions -- if a field wasn't
   returned by any provider, it's genuinely unknown, don't guess.
5. Report partial provider failures accurately (search_research's response includes
   provider_coverage and any partial_failures -- check them, don't assume every provider
   succeeded).
6. This server does not do arbitrary web browsing. retrieve_research_content only accepts a
   reference to a work whose access was already resolved -- it is not a general browse_url tool.

PREFERRED SEQUENCES:
- Topic discovery: search_research -> get_research_work (if reconciling one result in detail)
  -> resolve_research_access -> retrieve_research_content -> get_research_evidence (for
  citations).
- Known publication: get_research_work -> resolve_research_access -> retrieve_research_content
  -> get_research_evidence.
- Citation exploration: get_research_work -> find_related_research -> get_research_work (for
  selected related works) -> resolve_research_access only for the ones you'll actually use.
- Researcher discovery: search_research_author -> search_research constrained to that author ->
  get_research_work for selected works.

Each tool's own description (below, and in tools/list) repeats its specific use-when/do-not-use
guidance -- read those too, this is the shared overview.

tools.name: search_research
tools.title: Search Research
tools.description:
Search appropriate scholarly sources and return normalised, deduplicated, ranked research works.

Use when: Exploring a topic, finding publications, or beginning a literature search.
Do NOT use when: You already have a specific DOI/PMID/arXiv ID -- use get_research_work instead, it's more precise and cheaper.
Typically follows: (usually the first tool called for a new topic)
Typically followed by: get_research_work (to reconcile a specific result), resolve_research_access (before requesting content)
Side effects: Calls multiple provider APIs in parallel; no content acquisition happens here.

tools.name: get_research_work
tools.title: Get Research Work
tools.description:
Retrieve and reconcile one already-known work by identifier.

Use when: You have a DOI, PMID, PMCID, arXiv ID, OpenAlex ID, or Semantic Scholar ID -- or an earlier tool returned one.
Do NOT use when: You're exploring a topic with no specific paper in mind yet -- use search_research first.
Typically follows: search_research (to discover the identifier), or the user supplying one directly
Typically followed by: resolve_research_access, find_related_research
Side effects: None beyond the provider API call(s) needed to reconcile the identifier.

tools.name: find_related_research
tools.title: Find Related Research
tools.description:
Find cited, citing, or semantically related research for a known seed work, where the source provider supports it.

Use when: After identifying a seed paper and you want to explore its citation neighborhood.
Do NOT use when: As the first tool for an unconstrained topic search -- start with search_research instead.
Typically follows: get_research_work or search_research (to get a seed work)
Typically followed by: get_research_work (for selected related works), resolve_research_access (only for the ones you actually need content from)
Side effects: None beyond provider API calls; does not acquire content.

tools.name: search_research_author
tools.title: Search Research Author
tools.description:
Find and reconcile author records.

Use when: Researcher discovery, author disambiguation, or finding works by a specific author.
Do NOT use when: You already have the author's identifier and just want their works -- use search_research with preferred_sources scoped appropriately, or get_research_work per known paper.
Typically follows: (often a first tool, when the request is about a person rather than a topic)
Typically followed by: search_research (constrained to the resolved author), get_research_work
Side effects: None; no content acquisition.

tools.name: resolve_research_access
tools.title: Resolve Research Access
tools.description:
Determine whether metadata, abstract, public HTML, public PDF, or another approved content location is available for a work -- WITHOUT fetching it yet.

Use when: Before requesting full content for a specific work.
Do NOT use when: You only need metadata/abstract, which search_research/get_research_work already returned -- don't resolve access you won't use.
Typically follows: get_research_work or a result from search_research
Typically followed by: retrieve_research_content, but ONLY if the resolution actually found a usable location
Side effects: None -- this tool never fetches content, only decides where content might be.

tools.name: retrieve_research_content
tools.title: Retrieve Research Content
tools.description:
Retrieve and process content from an already-resolved, approved location.

Use when: After resolve_research_access found a usable location, and you actually need the full text (not just metadata) to answer the request.
Do NOT use when: A metadata record or abstract is already sufficient -- do not acquire content just because you can. Also never for arbitrary unrestricted URLs -- this tool does not accept a bare URL not tied to a resolved work.
Typically follows: resolve_research_access
Typically followed by: get_research_evidence, if you need to cite/verify how the content was obtained
Side effects: Performs a real network fetch (HTTP -> Crawl4AI -> bounded Playwright fallback), SSRF-protected. May be slow for the Playwright tier.

tools.name: get_research_evidence
tools.title: Get Research Evidence
tools.description:
Return provider provenance, source identifiers, access history, processing status, and evidence for a previously returned work.

Use when: Verifying a claim, generating citations, explaining source coverage, or showing how a result was actually obtained.
Do NOT use when: You haven't retrieved/resolved anything about this work yet -- there's nothing to show evidence for.
Typically follows: Any of the other tools, once you have a canonical_id to ask about.
Typically followed by: (usually the last tool in a chain, feeding the final answer's citations)
Side effects: None -- pure read of what already happened.

attempts.instructions:
This server extracts content from documents. It exposes exactly ONE tool, read_document --
there is no separate tool per engine or per OCR capability, and you never choose which
extraction engine runs. The server inspects each document and routes it automatically between
a fast path (MarkItDown) and an advanced/OCR path (Docling), retrying with the advanced path if
the fast path's output turns out insufficient. This is read-only: no document creation,
editing, or generation.

EXTRACTION_MODE:
- "auto" (default) -- the server decides fast vs advanced based on the document itself.
- "fast" -- prefer the lightweight path; may produce a worse result on a scanned/complex
  document (this will show up in `warnings`, not be silently upgraded).
- "advanced" -- force the more capable path (handles OCR, tables, complex layout).
- "ocr" -- force OCR-capable processing explicitly.

RESPONSE CONTRACT -- always check these fields, don't assume success from a lack of exception:
- `processing_status`: "completed" | "failed" | "rejected". A "rejected" status (e.g. a
  password-protected document, an unsupported file type, a blocked URI) is not the same as
  "failed" (a real processing failure) -- read `warnings` for why.
- `extraction_engine` and `ocr_used` tell you which path actually ran and whether OCR was
  involved -- don't assume based on the file type alone.
- `attempts` records every engine tried, including ones that were tried and rejected as
  insufficient before a fallback succeeded, with `fallback_reason` -- this server does not
  silently retry without telling you.
- `content` is empty/absent when `processing_status` is not "completed" -- never treat an empty
  response as "the document has no content" without checking `processing_status` first.

KNOWN, HONEST SCOPING (don't assume more than this actually does):
- `tables`/`images` are only populated when the advanced (Docling) path ran -- a
  fast-path-only extraction returns empty arrays even if the source document visibly has tables
  or images (they remain embedded in `content` as markdown, not extracted separately).
- `page_range` only has real effect on PDF input; it's a documented no-op (with a warning) for
  other formats.
- ZIP/archive files are not supported input in this version.
- This service does not currently perform malware scanning or enforce real user/agent
  authentication -- do not rely on it as the sole security boundary for untrusted input; treat
  it as read-only extraction over documents you already trust the source of.

tools.name: read_document
tools.title: Read Document
tools.description:
Read and extract content from a document. `uri` must be a file:// URI (restricted to a
configured allowed local root) or an https:// URI (restricted to an approved-domain
allowlist, SSRF-protected). extraction_mode: "auto" (default, server decides fast vs
advanced), "fast" (prefer MarkItDown), "advanced" (force Docling), "ocr" (force OCR-capable
processing). page_range (e.g. "3-7") only applies to PDF input. output_format: "markdown"
(default), "text", or "json" -- requesting "json" or include_tables=True on a PDF routes to
the advanced engine, since only it produces structured table data. Returns
{source_uri, file_name, file_type, page_count, processing_status, extraction_engine,
extraction_mode, ocr_used, detected_languages, content, tables, images, metadata, warnings,
attempts}. Check `processing_status` and `attempts` rather than assuming success -- a
"rejected" status means the request was refused (unsupported type, password-protected,
blocked URI), not a processing failure.
